title: Revisiting Subgradient Dominance in Robust MDPs: Counterexamples, Hardness, and Sufficient Conditions
claim: A small concrete instance shows the standard method fails: the objective landscape has a strictly suboptimal local minimum despite assumed favorable structure.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, state-transition graphs beside a contour heatmap with starred minima
description: The left panel shows two small deterministic MDP transition graphs, P1 and P2, each with three circular states: s1, s2 and s+. Blue arrows mark action a1 and red arrows mark action a2. Self-loops and cross transitions differ between the two kernels. A black arrow out of s+ carries cost c = +1. The right panel is a square contour heatmap of robust total cost J_P(π). The axes are π(a1|s1) and π(a1|s2), each running 0 to 1, and a viridis colorbar sits beside it. Contour lines are labeled with cost values. Two red stars mark local minima at opposite corners, one with cost 0.10 and one with cost 0.50, each labeled in small blue or red text. The eye goes first to the colorful landscape and the starred corners. Sub-captions sit under each panel.
caption: An RMDP where PSD fails (left) and its robust total cost landscape (right). The policy ${\color{red}\pi_2}$, which always selects action ${\color{red}a_2}$, is a strictly suboptimal local minimum. Details are provided in [ref].
abstract: Projected subgradient descent (PSD) has gained popularity for solving robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) because it applies to a broader class of uncertainty sets than traditional dynamic programming. Existing work claims that RMDPs with a general compact uncertainty set satisfy the subgradient dominance property, under which exact PSD finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy in a polynomial number of updates (e.g., Wang et al., 2023). We show that these claims are incorrect. Even when the uncertainty set has cardinality two, the RMDP objective need not be subgradient-dominant and can admit suboptimal strict local minima. Moreover, we prove that finding an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy can be NP-hard even in settings where subgradients are efficiently computable: (i) finite transition uncertainty sets and (ii) $sa$-rectangular finite transition uncertainty sets with finite non-rectangular cost uncertainty sets. Finally, we identify two conditions under which RMDPs do satisfy subgradient dominance: when, for each policy, either the worst-case transition kernel is unique or a robust action-value function exists.
